/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.headline: FAA announces first US digital air traffic control towers in Florida and Alaska
/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.excerpt: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US are officially operational, bringing new technology first to smaller airports in Florida and Alaska as the Trump administration presses ahead with updating the country’s ageing aviation infrastructure. The systems are now online at the Bartow executive airport (KBOW) in Florida and the Kenai municipal airport (PAEN) in Alaska, with five additional regional airports slated to receive the technology next. The digital towers use advanced camera systems and digital displays to give air traffic controllers a continuous, 360-degree view of airport operations, including runways, taxiways and surrounding airspace, according to the agency. The FAA maintains that the technology is not intended to replace human controllers. Instead, the systems are designed to provide greater visibility and additional information to help controllers perform their existing duties. “Our air traffic controllers continue to do the critical job of keeping aircraft safely separated, and we’re giving them better technology to do that,” said the FAA’s administrator, Bryan Bedford, in a statement. “Digital towers provide controllers with greater visibility of airport activity and more information to make critical decisions,” he added.
/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.trail: Systems provide 360-degree view of airport operations, but concerns have been raised about the technology

/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.headline: ‘No one’s here, no one knows’: north-east Ohio is ground zero for ICE flights
/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.excerpt: Just after 10.30am on a recent weekday morning, a Bombardier CRJ200 Air Wisconsin aircraft landed at Youngstown-Warren regional airport. Having made the 75-minute flight from Milwaukee, the 50-seater came to a halt and its twin engines fired down next to another Air Wisconsin plane and a larger Eastern Air Express Boeing 737, planes that flew in the evening before from Alexandria, Louisiana. Together, the planes – which combined can handle about 300 passengers at a time – and this austere, quiet airport a few miles from the Ohio-Pennsylvania state line, represent the cornerstone of the Trump administration’s Great Lakes deportation campaign. Last year, the facility, which handles no commercial flights, saw 398 “shuffle” – ICE-contracted flights between US airports – and direct deportation flights. With about 300 flights from this and the neighboring Akron-Canton regional airport respectively recorded so far this year by ICE Flights Monitor, an advocacy group, these small, often empty airports have seen more enforcement flights between US cities than many bigger metro areas. In fact, only seven other US airports this year have seen more deportation shuffle flights than the two combined. Turning these small airports into a key cog of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign has angered many.
/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground.trail: Away from the public eye, deportation planes at Youngstown-Warren and Akron-Canton airports carry hundreds of immigrants daily amid Trump’s ICE crackdown

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.headline: Tory and Reform politicians clash over migration as asylum centre approved
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.excerpt: Senior Tory and Reform politicians have clashed over immigration policy in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington after the government approved plans to convert a defence site into accommodation for asylum seekers. Zia Yusuf and Chris Philp raised their voices and spoke over each other in front of TV cameras and local people for more than three minutes. Yusuf urged his fellow home affairs spokesperson to apologise for his record as a minister. Philp said they should instead “stand in solidarity with residents” and Yusuf should “read the room”. The clash came hours after villagers said they would launch a legal challenge to plans to house more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers near them. It emerged on Thursday that Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, had approved full planning permission, a decision welcomed by the Home Office, which wants to end the use of asylum hotels. In their clash, Yusuf said: “Chris, would you like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into the country illegally?” Philp, who served as an immigration minister, said: “That is disingenuous, Zia, as usual … I hope today we can stand in solidarity with the residents.
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.trail: Chris Philp and Zia Yusuf trade barbs in Oxfordshire village planning legal action to block conversion of military base

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.headline: ‘Never thought I’d eat that’: how vegetable prescriptions are helping Britons with diabetes
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.excerpt: The participants admitted that throughout their life, their food choices had been far from ideal: egg and chips, hearty roasts, raw fry – a Cornish one-pan dish of bacon, potatoes and onions, often fried in lard and once beloved of miners and fishers. But here they were, at a community orchard in the harbourside town of St Ives in south-west Cornwall, massaging Swiss chard (to soften the leaves), dicing carrots, adding lentils into a pot to create a low-GI, high-fibre – and tasty – shepherd’s bake. The six people who worked together on the bake were taking part in a pioneering “veg on prescription” programme for patients with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, in which participants are given free weekly veg boxes and access to group cooking and gardening sessions. Many of the more than 100 people who have taken part in the WellFed scheme have reported improvements in their blood sugar levels, their weight and their feeling of wellbeing. Chris Longthorp, 74, one of those in the St Ives “chop and chat” session, said he had been surprised when he had been diagnosed with type 2, saying it had “crept up” on him. He described his usual diet as “standard fodder … meat and two veg, quite a lot of sweet things”. Since joining WellFed, Longthorp, who used to work in the pharmaceutical industry, said his HbA1c – blood glucose – level had dropped from 50 to 42. Diabetes UK says having a HbA1c over 48 risks complications such as problems in eyes, kidneys and feet.
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.trail: WellFed participants in Cornwall report better blood sugar levels with help of free veg boxes, cooking and gardening

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.headline: Leeds woman, 18, admits knife murder of 16-year-old love rival
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.excerpt: An 18-year-old woman who stabbed a teenage girl to death during a planned fight over a young man has pleaded guilty to murder. Chloe Watson Dransfield, 16, was attacked by Kayla Smith, 18, after going to the latter’s home with her boyfriend Blake Dowling in Leeds, West Yorkshire, a court heard. Smith had pleaded guilty to manslaughter but denied murder. She then changed her plea to guilty on the second day of her trial at Leeds crown court on Thursday. Dowling, 18, who took Chloe to the house, and Archie Rycroft, 20, who followed Smith to the fight on 28 March, are also charged with murder and manslaughter and their trial will continue. They both deny the charges against them. The judge, Mr Justice Cavanagh KC, said he would sentence Smith when the trial concluded, adding the only sentence he could give was life imprisonment but he would need to set the minimum term she must spend in custody. The trial previously heard Dowling had been in a relationship with both Chloe and Smith and “knew of the bad feeling between the two females”, although they had never met in person before the fatal attack. Dowling’s mother told the court Smith was “jealous and obsessed” over her son’s relationship with Chloe. The prosecution said Chloe and Smith had argued over the phone the previous evening, with Smith threatening to “stab her” several times.

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.headline: Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.excerpt: Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services. Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK. These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner. The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why. Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime. The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat. Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International.
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/david-walliams-alle.trail: Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.headline: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.excerpt: Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month. The prime minister told MPs the UK would bring further sanctions against Tehran and the IRGC in the aftermath of an ambiguous episode that, despite over a fortnight of police investigation, has yet to lead to anybody being charged. Addressing parliament on Monday about events at RAF Fairford, Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards.” In a statement to the House of Commons, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, told MPs that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had summoned the Iranian ambassador over the Fairford incident and that the government had imposed sanctions on two individuals accused of spying in Europe and the US. “He [Miliband] will condemn Iran’s continued attempts to undermine our safety. We are also sanctioning two individuals involved in conducting espionage and attacks on behalf of the government of Iran in Europe and the US, and we will not hesitate to take further action to restrict Iran’s capacity to threaten international security,” she said. Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September.

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.headline: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.excerpt: Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran. The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before. Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”. Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening. US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US. A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year. But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away.
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.trail: A dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from Iran

/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.headline: US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
/uk-news/2026/nov/13/us-air-force-respon.excerpt: The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base. The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity. A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While ⁠operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in ‌real time, we can acknowledge ‌now that all US bombers that were deployed to ‌RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.” At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat. There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire. According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base. A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.

/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.headline: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.excerpt: Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world? Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run. This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading. Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft, Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes. What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself. One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments. In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI.
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.trail: CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus

/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.headline: Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.excerpt: Microsoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the latest example of how AI is reshaping tech companies and the greater workforce. This is the latest of several trimmings Microsoft has made to its workforce this year. The company announced in April that it was offering voluntary retirement to about 7% of its US workforce, which consisted of about 125,000 employees at the time. Its global workforce is made up of about 223,000 workers globally. Some of Microsoft’s most recognizable divisions – including Xbox, Windows and Copilot, its AI tool – will be participating in the offer, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Employees in certain divisions, including in cybersecurity, datacenters and marketing, would not be eligible for the offer, it said. “This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice-president and chief people officer, said in a statement. The company did not respond to a request for comment on further details about the offer. Multiple tech companies have announced layoffs due to the rise of AI and increased investment in the technology this year.
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.trail: Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports

/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.headline: Microsoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.excerpt: The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies. The development by the British company Nscale, heralded by ministers as the country’s largest AI datacentre when it was announced in 2025, was planned to open at Loughton in Essex next year. Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardian revealed in March that the location was still an operational scaffolding yard. Now there are further concerns after Microsoft, one of its largest planned customers and expected to have been the anchor tenant, informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement. It comes a month after it emerged that power supply problems meant the project would face a lengthy wait before coming online. Keir Starmer’s government had highlighted the Loughton project when announcing the UK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing it as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots. The end of the deal with Microsoft, first reported in the Telegraph, means Nscale has lost its only publicly announced customer for the Essex datacentre. It is understood that Microsoft remains on board for another project the company has in Norway.
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.trail: Development by UK firm Nscale heralded by ministers as largest of its kind in country loses anchor tenant

/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.headline: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.excerpt: Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC. Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”. He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions.
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.trail: Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents

/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.headline: ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.excerpt: Apple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models. It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rush hoovering up every memory chip available for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips and other critical components for electronics, including phones. The situation has dramatically driven up costs, with some chips five times dearer than previously listed. Therefore the everyday electronics products people rely on are suddenly significantly more expensive to make, and that is being passed on to consumers. “Two things are happening at once,” says Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of client devices at research company IDC. “Component costs have risen sharply, with memory alone up more than 300% year on year.” Because older iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones, Apple is pricing them as current products, he adds. The iPhone is not the first product to have a RAMageddon price increase, but it is the single biggest-selling electrical product in the world. For many, this means the real cost of the AI splurge will be £100 without getting anything more for your money.
/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage.trail: Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper

/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.headline: Vetting candidates is a tricky process but Reform can’t seem to get it right
/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.excerpt: Speaking to reporters after unveiling his new defence spokesperson this week, Nigel Farage’s jovial and upbeat mood suddenly switched. Why, he was asked, was a Reform UK councillor who was arrested in January over multiple alleged sexual offences still in his role nearly 10 months later? “I have no idea,” Farage replied icily. “I was told yesterday, and I wasn’t very happy.” A later question about Reform’s misfiring processes for vetting candidates did nothing to improve the mood. Why, Farage asked, was wrongdoing in other parties barely covered, when the news that the arrested Reform councillor had been charged prompted a BBC News alert? In fairness to the BBC, the charges brought against George Madgwick, who was Reform’s leader on Hampshire county council, were many and deeply serious, 35 in all, including 12 allegations of rape. Madgwick has said he is innocent. But more generally, it is another difficult moment for a party that has had to expand and professionalise at unprecedented speed, a process that its internal structures have at times failed to keep up with. Little more than a week earlier, it emerged that a member of Farage’s security team, Ryan Dinnage, who was with him during this year’s local elections campaign, was facing a rape charge at the time for which he was later convicted and jailed. Reform UK said they were unaware of the charge and that Dinnage “ceased to be used” by the party when it came to light.
/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.trail: Charges against party members and off-piste remarks highlight problems brought about by rapid expansion

/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.headline: EHRC raises concern with Reform about ‘racial and sexual remarks’ in documentary
/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.excerpt: The official equalities watchdog has written to Reform UK to raise concerns after an undercover TV documentary showed councillors and candidates for the party expressing racist and misogynistic views, with one of the party’s MPs complaining about ingrained sexism. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it had written to Nigel Farage’s party in the wake of revelations in ITV’s Undercover: A Year in Reform, which was broadcast in October. While Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, footage in the programme included Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, making Islamophobic remarks, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues. In another section, the Reform MP Sarah Pochin was shown complaining that the party was “chauvinistic” and riven with “alpha male shit”. An EHRC statement said its letter had asked Reform to provide information, “including what action the party is taking to comply with the Equality Act”.
/politics/2026/nov/13/nigel-farage-perso.trail: Watchdog writes to Nigel Farage’s party to ask what action it is taking to comply with the Equality Act

/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.headline: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.excerpt: When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions. “I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.” Rhys was in the grips of drug addiction and turned to shoplifting to fund his habit. He had struggled with drug use since he was a teenager and then, in 2019, he took crack cocaine for the first time. “Within a week, I was going into shops and shoplifting for it, because you just can’t get enough,” he said. Over the next few years, he shoplifted 10-15 times a day and was sent to prison several times. However, without help to tackle his addiction, Rhys struggled to change his behaviour. “I’d spend hours shoplifting but, at the end of the day, I still wouldn’t have anything to eat. I’d be jumping back over the fence to go through the bins to get myself a sandwich. I wouldn’t even get myself a bottle of water,” he said. “My priority was always getting the stuff to sell for drugs.” On Wednesday, the home secretary announced plans to target 500 of the most prolific shoplifters across the country with police crackdowns in 17 areas. Measures include banning repeat offenders from high streets and town centres, closer monitoring of offenders with regular hearings before a judge and the use of electronic tagging.
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.trail: Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment

/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.headline: Domestic violence survivor living ‘in terror’ after attacker released without tag
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.excerpt: A domestic violence survivor who was punched, threatened with a knife and had her front door kicked in by her former partner has been “living in terror” because he had still not been fitted with a tracking tag, weeks after his release from prison. Michelle, 38, who now lives in a static caravan with her four children, said relatives were sleeping on her floor in case the man tried to attack again. He had been recalled to prison on several occasions before for breaching his probation conditions. “The police and probation know that he is a threat to me and has breached the terms of his probation before. It is as if they are waiting for something really bad to happen to me or my children before they help,” she said this weekend. Days after being contacted for comment by the Guardian, a government source on Monday said that the man has now been fitted with two electronic monitors – a GPS tag and an alcohol tag. The source said there was “no causal link” between the Guardian’s queries and the tag being fitted. Michelle was among hundreds of domestic violence survivors who demanded to know why tags are not being fitted on offenders as they leave prison. Instead, the private-sector firm Serco is being contracted to fit them after they have been released. “They should be tagged as soon as they come out,” Michelle said. “Who knows where violent people are going to go and what they are going to do?

/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.headline: More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.excerpt: More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday. Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released. A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total. The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month. The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis. The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said. The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026.
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.trail: Ministry of Justice figures show recalls rose 27% in year to June despite emergency measures to ease overcrowding

/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.headline: Shabana Mahmood urged to grant visa to former Weather Underground activist
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.excerpt: Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour. Judith Clark, 77, was the inspiration for Walter’s portrayal of prisoners in the Donmar Warehouse all-female Shakespeare trilogy, including Brutus in Julius Caesar and Prospero in The Tempest. Clark had been invited to speak about rehabilitation and restorative justice at a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Julius Caesar in Stratford-upon-Avon next month, but her application to visit Britain was refused last week. She had also hoped to attend the UK launch of her daughter Harriet Clark’s first novel, The Hill, on 5 November. Kennedy said that while the Home Office had rules governing visas for people with serious criminal convictions, there was also ministerial discretion, which should be exercised in Clark’s case. “This is a woman in her 70s who served a long sentence for political activism, which involved no violence on her part, and whose clear remorse and exceptional works within the prison system led to her early release,” she said.

/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.headline: Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.excerpt: Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales. The imposition of new prison sanctions, coming into effect next year, builds on existing laws that order offenders to attend sentencing or face a fine or be jailed for a further two years for contempt of court. “Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences,” said the prisons minister, Catherine McKinnell. The new rules, to be laid before parliament on Thursday, will grant judges new powers to impose a loss of prison privileges for 84 days, cell confinement for 21 days, a loss of social visits for 27 days and a restriction on visits to once every four weeks, for 84 days. They could result in offenders already facing decades behind bars facing additional punishments. The Ministry of Justice has said that while no measure could guarantee offenders would attend their sentencing hearing, the widened powers strengthened the consequences for offenders and ensured they could be “appropriately punished”. Pia Sinha, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, raised questions for ministers as to whether the new rules would achieve the aim of getting offenders to attend sentence hearings.
/society/2026/nov/13/probation-officers-.trail: England and Wales judges to be able to keep inmates in cells for longer or stop visits if they refuse to face victims’ families in court

A 2020 report by the US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence investigating Russian interference in the 2016 US presidential election identified Zavorotniy as an officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) involved in influence operations. That explosion occurred on Thursday morning in the city’s Pushkinsky district, an area home to many military personnel, according to law enforcement officials and media reports.

/world/2026/nov/14/ukraine-war-briefing-.excerpt: Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service. During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed. He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”. Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026. The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks. Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow. The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.
